counterexample: Take n=2, p=-2, q=-1, x_1=1, x_2=2. Then p<q, and the required positivity condition for p<0 holds. Both exponents are finite and nonzero, so lines 0005–0029 do not cover this case; neither exponent is zero, so lines 0031–0039 do not cover it; and p,q are not in R_{>=0}, contrary to line 0040's claim that only that case remains. Explicitly, M_{-2}=((1+1/4)/2)^{-1/2}=sqrt(8/5) and M_{-1}=((1+1/2)/2)^{-1}=4/3, but the proof supplies no argument comparing them.
assessment_summary: Line 0040 unjustifiably restricts the remaining finite-exponent cases to nonnegative p and q. It omits all p<q<0 cases (and also cases crossing zero), so the subsequent Jensen argument cannot establish the theorem in full.
